power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Urinary tract infections are commonly caused by bacteria whose antibiotic susceptibility varies between clinical settings. 1 We studied urinary isolates from 95 patients with suspected infection at Lahore General Hospital, Pakistan, between July and December 2023.
text.formatted: Urinary tract infections are commonly caused by bacteria whose antibiotic susceptibility varies between clinical settings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> We studied urinary isolates from 95 patients with suspected infection at Lahore General Hospital, Pakistan, between July and December 2023.

text.text: Urine culture showed significant bacterial growth in 63 specimens (66.3%).
Escherichia coli accounted for 30 isolates, followed by 18 Klebsiella isolates, comprising 16 Klebsiella pneumoniae and two Klebsiella oxytoca.
Klebsiella was recovered from 12 female and six male patients, and the largest number of Klebsiella isolates occurred in patients aged 21-30 years.
The aggregate susceptibility results, recorded for 18 isolates per antibiotic, showed the highest susceptibility to imipenem and meropenem (17/18 each), followed by nitrofurantoin (16/18).
Resistance to several cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides was frequent.
These findings describe the bacterial distribution and reported susceptibility patterns in a small hospital sample.
Larger studies with verified species-specific susceptibility data are needed before these findings can guide local treatment policy.
Urinary tract infections affect the bladder, urethra and kidneys and are encountered in both community and hospital practice.
Their clinical presentation ranges from lower urinary symptoms to systemic infection.

Diagnosis requires consideration of symptoms, patient characteristics and laboratory findings. 2 Differences in underlying illness and infection severity also influence how susceptibility data should be interpreted across patient groups. 3 Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important urinary pathogen, particularly in patients with underlying illness or impaired host defences. 4 Its capsule, adhesins, iron-acquisition systems and capacity to form biofilms contribute to colonisation and persistence. 5 Extended-spectrum β-lactamases and carbapenemases can limit the antibiotics available for treatment. 6, 7 These mechanisms cannot, however, be inferred from a susceptibility percentage alone.
text.formatted: Diagnosis requires consideration of symptoms, patient characteristics and laboratory findings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> Differences in underlying illness and infection severity also influence how susceptibility data should be interpreted across patient groups. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important urinary pathogen, particularly in patients with underlying illness or impaired host defences. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> Its capsule, adhesins, iron-acquisition systems and capacity to form biofilms contribute to colonisation and persistence. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> Extended-spectrum β-lactamases and carbapenemases can limit the antibiotics available for treatment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> These mechanisms cannot, however, be inferred from a susceptibility percentage alone.

text.text: Studies from South Punjab, Timurgara, Karachi and Quetta have described antibiotic resistance among urinary pathogens in Pakistan. 8, 9, 10, 11 Their findings support the use of local laboratory data, because the distribution of organisms and their susceptibility patterns vary between hospitals and patient populations.
text.formatted: Studies from South Punjab, Timurgara, Karachi and Quetta have described antibiotic resistance among urinary pathogens in Pakistan. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> Their findings support the use of local laboratory data, because the distribution of organisms and their susceptibility patterns vary between hospitals and patient populations.

text.text: Studies of Klebsiella elsewhere have also documented variation in resistance, virulence characteristics and genetic diversity. 12, 13 This study examined urine specimens from patients with suspected urinary tract infection at Lahore General Hospital.
text.formatted: Studies of Klebsiella elsewhere have also documented variation in resistance, virulence characteristics and genetic diversity. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> This study examined urine specimens from patients with suspected urinary tract infection at Lahore General Hospital.

text.text: The objectives were to describe the frequency of Klebsiella among recovered organisms and summarise the reported antibiotic susceptibility of the isolates.
A cross-sectional study was conducted at Lahore General Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan, from July to December 2023.
Patients with suspected urinary tract infection were recruited using nonprobability convenience sampling.
Both sexes and all age groups were eligible.
The study 2 included 95 patients.
The sample size was based on an anticipated proportion of 0.14, a 95% confidence level and an absolute precision of 0.07, using n = Z²P(1 -P)/d².
The planned sample size was 95.
Patients without suspected infection, patients with the chronic diseases listed in the study protocol, and improperly labelled or contaminated specimens were excluded.
Urine specimens were collected in sterile screw-capped containers after patients were instructed to clean the external genital area.
Specimens were transported to the microbiology laboratory within one hour.

Samples awaiting examination were refrigerated at 4-8 °C. Urine was inoculated onto cysteine-lactose-electrolyte-deficient agar and incubated aerobically overnight at 37 °C. Cultures were assessed for significant bacterial growth.
Cultured organisms were examined by Gram staining and biochemical testing.
The described tests included urease production, citrate utilisation, triple sugar iron agar reactions, indole production, motility and oxidase activity.
An API 20E identification system was also described.
Inoculated API strips were incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours, and reaction codes were compared with the manufacturer's identification catalogue.
Susceptibility was assessed by the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method on Mueller-Hinton agar (Hi-Media).
Three to five colonies were suspended in sterile saline and adjusted to a turbidity standard.

The suspension was spread across the agar surface, antibiotic discs were applied, and plates were incubated aerobically overnight at 35 °C. Inhibition-zone diameters were measured with a calibrated scale and interpreted using a zone-interpretation chart.
The tested agents and recorded susceptible and resistant counts are listed in Table 3 Percentages in the tables and figures were calculated from the reported counts and rounded to one decimal place.
text.formatted: The tested agents and recorded susceptible and resistant counts are listed in Table <ref type="table">3</ref> Percentages in the tables and figures were calculated from the reported counts and rounded to one decimal place.

text.text: No inferential tests or treatment-outcome analyses were reported.
The study included 95 patients: 55 females (57.9%) and 40 males (42.1%).
Significant bacterial growth was reported in specimens (66.3%); the remaining 32 specimens (33.7%) were culture negative (Table 1).
text.formatted: Significant bacterial growth was reported in 63 specimens (66.3%); the remaining 32 specimens (33.7%) were culture negative (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: These percentages describe the recruited hospital sample and do not estimate the prevalence of urinary tract infection in the wider population.

Sex-specific Klebsiella percentages are descriptive and were calculated from the reported counts; no significance test is presented.
Escherichia coli was the most frequently recovered organism, with 30 isolates (47.6% of the 63 isolates).

Klebsiella accounted for 18 isolates (28.6%), followed by Staphylococcus species (7; 11.1%), Enterococcus (5; 7.9%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (2; 3.2%) and Proteus mirabilis (1; 1.6%) (Table 2 and Fig. 1).

text.text: Gram-negative organisms accounted for 51 isolates (81.0%) and Gram-positive organisms for 12 (19.0%).
Of the 18 Klebsiella isolates, 16 (88.9%) were identified as K. pneumoniae and two (11.1%) as K. oxytoca.
Klebsiella was recovered from 12 female and six male patients, corresponding to 21.8% of the 55 females and 15.0% of the 40 males.
These were descriptive comparisons; no test of a sex-associated difference was reported.
The largest number of Klebsiella isolates occurred in patients aged 21-30 years (8/18; 44.4%), followed by those aged 31-40 years (4/18; 22.2%).
Two isolates each were reported in the 11-20 and 41-50 year groups, and one each in the youngest reported group and the 51-60 year group.
Age-specific infection risk could not be estimated because the numbers of all recruited patients in each age group were not available.

The susceptibility results contained 18 observations for each antibiotic (Table 3 and Fig. 2).
text.formatted: The susceptibility results contained 18 observations for each antibiotic (Table <ref type="table">3</ref> and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: Imipenem and meropenem each had 17 susceptible isolates (94.4%), followed by nitrofurantoin with 16 (88.9%) and fosfomycin with 14 (77.8%).
Amikacin had four susceptible isolates (22.2%), while tobramycin and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid each had three (16.7%).
Gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, cefotaxime, ceftazidime and tigecycline each had two susceptible isolates (11.1%) and 16 resistant isolates (88.9%).
The agent recorded as tazobactam (TZP) had one susceptible isolate and 17 resistant isolates.
Its exact antibiotic formulation requires confirmation.
The aggregate results do not separate K. pneumoniae from K. oxytoca.

These descriptive results do not establish clinical treatment efficacy.
Klebsiella was the second most frequently recovered bacterial group after E. coli in this hospital sample.
Culture positivity was 66.3%, while Klebsiella accounted for 28.6% of recovered isolates and 18.9% of all sampled patients.
These denominators answer different questions and should not be used interchangeably.
Reports from Pakistan and other settings also identify E. coli and Klebsiella among urinary pathogens, although their relative frequencies vary.
The high reported susceptibility to imipenem and meropenem is consistent with some earlier studies of urinary Klebsiella isolates.

Polse and colleagues reported susceptibility to both agents, and studies from Iraq and India also described activity of imipenem against urinary isolates. 15, 16, 17 However, those studies differed in patient selection, collection period and testing procedures.
text.formatted: Polse and colleagues reported susceptibility to both agents, and studies from Iraq and India also described activity of imipenem against urinary isolates. <ref type="bibr">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> However, those studies differed in patient selection, collection period and testing procedures.

text.text: The present results should therefore be regarded as a local descriptive observation rather than a basis for recommending carbapenems for empirical treatment.
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin also showed relatively high reported susceptibility in this sample.

Other studies have described variation in the activity of urinary antibiotics between organisms and clinical settings. 18, 19 A laboratory susceptibility result does not by itself establish suitability for every urinary syndrome.
text.formatted: Other studies have described variation in the activity of urinary antibiotics between organisms and clinical settings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> A laboratory susceptibility result does not by itself establish suitability for every urinary syndrome.

text.text: Patient characteristics, the site and severity of infection, and validated interpretation of the laboratory result remain necessary when selecting treatment. 3 Resistance to the tested cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and several aminoglycosides was frequent.
text.formatted: Patient characteristics, the site and severity of infection, and validated interpretation of the laboratory result remain necessary when selecting treatment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> Resistance to the tested cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and several aminoglycosides was frequent.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with the concern about restricted treatment options described in studies of resistant Klebsiella infections. 12, 13, 20 The study did not include molecular testing or a reported confirmatory test for extended-spectrum β-lactamase or carbapenemase production.
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with the concern about restricted treatment options described in studies of resistant Klebsiella infections. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> The study did not include molecular testing or a reported confirmatory test for extended-spectrum β-lactamase or carbapenemase production.

text.text: Specific resistance mechanisms therefore cannot be assigned to these isolates.

Studies of hypervirulent and invasive K. pneumoniae have shown that clinical presentation, underlying illness and bacterial characteristics are relevant to interpretation. 21, 22, 23 None of those findings establishes that the isolates in the present study were hypervirulent.
text.formatted: Studies of hypervirulent and invasive K. pneumoniae have shown that clinical presentation, underlying illness and bacterial characteristics are relevant to interpretation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> None of those findings establishes that the isolates in the present study were hypervirulent.

text.text: The available data describe culture identification and aggregate susceptibility; they do not describe virulence genes, transmission, treatment response or mortality.
Species identification also matters.
Two of the 18 Klebsiella isolates were reported as K.
oxytoca, and the susceptibility results could not be separated by species.
Studies comparing 10.

conventional and genotypic identification methods illustrate the need to confirm organism identification when interpreting Klebsiella data. 24 Future surveillance should retain isolate-level species identification alongside each antibiotic result.
text.formatted: conventional and genotypic identification methods illustrate the need to confirm organism identification when interpreting Klebsiella data. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> Future surveillance should retain isolate-level species identification alongside each antibiotic result.

text.text: More Klebsiella isolates were recovered from females than males, but females also made up a larger proportion of the recruited patients.
The relevant descriptive proportions were 12/55 and 6/40, rather than the shares of females and males among the 18 positive patients.
The findings do not establish a sex-related risk difference.
Broader guidance on recurrent infection in women likewise depends on clinical history and the population being assessed, rather than isolate counts alone. 25
text.formatted: Broader guidance on recurrent infection in women likewise depends on clinical history and the population being assessed, rather than isolate counts alone. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref>

text.text: This was a small, single-hospital study using convenience sampling.
Only 18 Klebsiella isolates were reported, so a change in the result for one isolate changes an antibiotic percentage by approximately 5.6 percentage points.
The aggregate data did not allow species-specific susceptibility estimates or assessment of multidrug resistance in individual isolates.
Age-group denominators, molecular resistance data and treatment outcomes were unavailable.
Patientreported symptoms, medication history and previous antibiotic use could also have introduced reporting error.
The susceptibility categories require verification against the laboratory's original antibiotic-specific interpretive criteria.
E. coli was the most frequently recovered organism, followed by Klebsiella, in urine specimens from patients at Lahore General Hospital.
The reported aggregate Klebsiella results showed higher susceptibility to imipenem, meropenem, nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin than to several 11 other tested agents.
These findings support continued local surveillance, with clear species identification, validated susceptibility interpretation and linkage to clinical outcomes.
Ethical clearance was obtained from an ethical review board.
Permission was obtained from the Institute of Public Health, Lahore, and the study setting.
Patient consent was obtained before specimen collection and data recording.
This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.
The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
The authors declare no competing interests.

Muhammad Mohsin Khan reviewed the analysis and reviewed and edited the manuscript for content and language.
Syeda Rija Rashid contributed to the methodology, including sampling and susceptibility testing.
All authors read and approved the final manuscript.
